title: The consequences of netting
excerpt: What will change now that the net metering scheme will remain in place? In this blog, we explain what you can expect in this regard.
contentHtml:
What will change now that the netting scheme is being phased out? In this blog we explain what you can expect about this.

Still abolition of netting

For some time now there were plans to slowly phase out the netting scheme in the Netherlands from 2025. The netting scheme was originally intended to make solar panels less expensive for households. Because it allows users to cross the power they supply to the mains against the power they receive, they can more easily recoup their solar panels via the annual power savings.
Minister Jetten planned to phase out the netting scheme from 2025, as sufficient households have benefited from it. In the Senate, however, this plan has been voted down. However, the new cabinet plans to completely abolish the netting scheme from 2027. In the autumn, decision-making is on the agenda to finalize the plans of the new cabinet. What other consequences does this decision have?

Actions by energy companies

First of all, the netting scheme is bad news for energy companies. Generated electricity is mainly returned during the afternoon, when the supply is much greater than the demand. The netting itself is done on an annual basis, so that electricity that is returned in the summer is streaked away against more expensive electricity in the winter. In this way, the netting provides extra costs for energy companies. These costs can be handled in different ways. One possibility is to increase standard rates, so that customers without solar panels have to pay extra.
Another option is the system introduced by the Vandebron company; charge costs for the return of electricity, so-called return costs or even feed-in. A certain amount must be paid for each kWh that is returned, and with larger quantities on an annual basis, the amount per kWh increases. This means that netting is ultimately less profitable, as solar panel users still incur additional costs by returning power. The other energy companies now use comparable rates.

Influence on the net

Delivery back has another drawback; an increase in net congestion. If many users of solar panels in a district simultaneously supply power to the grid, the low-voltage grid can become overloaded. This means that the converters of solar panels turn off automatically, so that no power can be produced anymore. As a result, users no longer benefit from their solar cells. This usually happens on days with a lot of sunlight, especially the days when users should be of extra use to their solar panels.
Net congestion can be remedied by strengthening the grid, but it takes a lot of time and money, and as more and more people take solar panels, more improvements may be needed. Thus, using generated power itself as much as possible is the best way to prevent grid congestion. Of course this is not always possible, since on working days there is mainly power available when few people are at home. This also makes it more important to be able to store energy for later use. This is the intention of the WaterAccu from Solyx Energy, a combination of an electric boiler and a control device, the Solar iBoost.

Simple form of energy storage

In contrast to a home battery, a Water Battery stores current in the form of tap water. During the day, unused solar power is used via the Solar iBoost to heat tap water, so that it can be used for showering, washing dishes, etc. in the evening and / or morning. This not only improves the own use of generated electricity, but also reduces the gas consumption if the water were heated by a central heating boiler.
As mentioned earlier, delivery is less interesting in the meantime, and if net congestion is more common, delivery back will be even less possible. It is therefore a good idea to look at ways to use solar power as much as possible within the household, and the Water Battery is a simple solution!
